chapters.title: Language for interacting with others, and text structure

points.title: Language and identity
points.brief: The words we use, such as slang, local sayings and idioms, show who we are and which groups we belong to.

points.title: Evaluative language
points.brief: Words that judge a text or show a feeling about it, such as gripping, clumsy or moving, and how a fair judgement is backed up with details from the text.

points.title: Text structure follows purpose
points.brief: Texts are built to suit their purpose. A review moves from what the text is about to a judgement, and a persuasive text states a position, gives reasons, then sums up.

points.title: Introductions, topic sentences and conclusions
points.brief: An overview or introduction tells readers what is coming, a topic sentence opens each paragraph with its main idea, and a conclusion draws the ideas together.

points.title: Text connectives
points.brief: Words and phrases such as firstly, however, as a result and finally link ideas and show readers how one part of a text leads to the next.

points.title: Simple, compound and complex sentences
points.brief: A simple sentence has one main clause, a compound sentence joins two main clauses with words like and or but, and a complex sentence adds a dependent clause starting with words like because or when.

points.title: Compound-complex sentences
points.brief: A compound-complex sentence has at least two main clauses and one dependent clause, which lets a writer add a reason or condition and extend an idea in one sentence.

points.title: Keeping verb tense consistent
points.brief: Writers keep verbs in the same tense unless the time really changes, so a story told in the past tense does not slip into the present by mistake.

points.title: Using colons
points.brief: A colon comes after a complete clause to introduce a list, an example or an explanation of what came before.

points.title: Using brackets
points.brief: Brackets hold extra information, such as a date or a short explanation, that the sentence still makes sense without.

points.title: Vectors in images
points.brief: Vectors are lines in an image, such as a pointing arm, a road or a gaze, that lead the viewer's eye to what the creator wants noticed.

points.title: Camera angles
points.brief: A high angle looks down and can make a subject seem small or weak, a low angle looks up and can make it seem powerful, and eye level feels equal.

points.title: Social distance in images
points.brief: How close a subject appears changes how we relate to it. A close-up feels personal, a mid shot feels social and a long shot keeps the viewer at a distance.

points.title: Technical and everyday meanings
points.brief: Each subject has its own technical words, and some everyday words, such as cell, volume or table, take on a special meaning in a subject.

chapters.title: Literature and contexts, and responding to literature

points.title: Ideas, issues and points of view
points.brief: Literary texts explore ideas and issues, such as friendship or fairness, through characters and events, and each text tells its story from a point of view.

points.title: Literature from different contexts
points.brief: Readers meet stories, poems and plays from many times and places, including works by First Nations Australian authors, and the context a text comes from shapes what it shows.

points.title: Forming and justifying an opinion
points.brief: A response to a character, setting or event states an opinion and backs it with reasons and details from the text, even when others see it differently.

points.title: How dialogue builds character
points.brief: What characters say, and how they say it, shows their personality and feelings and can make readers like, pity or distrust them.

points.title: Words for talking about texts
points.brief: Metalanguage is the set of terms used to discuss texts, such as narrator, setting, imagery and theme, which make a response clear and precise.

points.title: Character, setting and events together
points.brief: In a narrative, characters, the setting and the events work together, so a stormy setting or a sudden event can reveal what a character is like.

points.title: Narrative structure
points.brief: Many narratives move from an orientation to a complication, rising action, a climax and a resolution.

points.title: Simile, metaphor and personification
points.brief: A simile compares using like or as, a metaphor says one thing is another, and personification gives human qualities to something that is not human.

points.title: Sound devices in poetry
points.brief: Poets use alliteration, assonance, onomatopoeia, rhyme and rhythm to create sound effects that add meaning and mood.

points.title: Imagery and layers of meaning
points.brief: Imagery appeals to the senses to help readers picture a scene, and a single image can hold more than one meaning at once.

points.title: Show, don't tell
points.brief: In their own stories, writers show a feeling through actions, details and dialogue rather than naming it outright.

chapters.title: Texts in context and interacting with others

points.title: How technology changes reading
points.brief: Digital texts use links, scrolling, video and comments, which change how people read, create and respond to texts such as news and social media.

points.title: Discussion skills
points.brief: Good discussion means listening, building on others' ideas, asking questions and disagreeing politely with reasons.

points.title: Using your voice in a presentation
points.brief: Speakers vary volume, tone, pitch and pace to hold attention and make their meaning clear.

points.title: Language features suit audience and purpose
points.brief: Writers choose words and features to suit who they are writing for and why, so a text for children reads differently from a report for adults.

points.title: Ways to organise ideas
points.brief: Texts can arrange ideas in time order, as causes and effects, or as groups and sub-groups, called a taxonomy.

points.title: Making inferences
points.brief: An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues in a text, such as a character's actions, when the writer does not say it directly.

points.title: Summarising
points.brief: A summary gives the main ideas of a text briefly in your own words and leaves out minor details and examples.

points.title: Predicting and questioning while reading
points.brief: Good readers predict what will come next, ask questions as they read and check whether they still understand.

points.title: Text purposes
points.brief: Texts can be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive or analytical, and the purpose shapes the structure and language a writer chooses.

points.title: Planning, drafting and editing
points.brief: Writers plan their ideas, write a draft, then edit for meaning, structure, spelling and punctuation before publishing.

points.title: Greek and Latin roots
points.brief: Many English words are built from Greek and Latin roots, such as bio for life and port for carry, which help readers spell and work out new words.

points.title: Prefixes, suffixes and base words
points.brief: A prefix goes before a base word and a suffix after it, changing its meaning or word class, as in unhappy and happiness.
